You are a requirements analyst at the start of a software project. Nobody has designed the service yet. Below are the full transcripts of three interviews with its future users: a fleet technician, a dispatcher, and the platform's airspace desk. The transcripts are everything you know about these users and their world.

=== TRANSCRIPTS ===
# Interview — a fleet technician

Interviewer: Could you walk me through your last working day as a fleet technician, starting from the moment you arrived and going until you left?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: No problem, let's start smaller. What was the first thing you did when you last started a shift?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: That's fine. Can you think of the last drone you worked on? What were you doing with it?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: I may be asking this in a way that's hard to answer. Is there something about your work that you'd rather start with?

Interviewee: I keep our drones and charging equipment in working order. I add new drones to our fleet, retire old ones, set up our charging pads at our sites, and take drones out of service for repairs and put them back. I also send drones to charge, and regulators can ask our company to show how our drones have been looked after.

Interviewer: Thank you, that helps. Tell me about the last time you took a drone out of service. What happened, from the moment you found out?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: How do you usually find out that a drone needs to come out of service?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: You mentioned that regulators can ask your company to show how drones have been looked after. What do you do when that happens?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Where do you keep the record of work you have done on a drone?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What part of your job worries you the most?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Who do you talk to most often during your work?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What would you most like me to understand about your work?

Interviewee: I keep drones and charging equipment in working order, and I add new drones to the fleet, retire old ones, and set up charging pads at our sites. I also take drones out of service for repairs, put them back, and send drones to charge.

Interviewer: You said you send drones to charge. How do you decide which drone gets charged?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Roughly how many drones are in your fleet?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What happens when you retire a drone?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: If a drone has a problem during a job, what do you want to know first?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Do you work alone, or with other people?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What makes these questions hard to answer?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Has there been a day recently when you went home frustrated?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Tell me about the last charging pad you set up at a site.

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Is there anything in your work that you double-check yourself?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When you put a drone back into service after a repair, what do you do just before?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What comes to mind when you hear that a new service is being built for the work you do?

Interviewee: I keep drones and charging equipment in working order, and I add new drones to the fleet, retire old ones, set up charging pads at our sites, and take drones out of service for repairs and put them back. I also send drones to charge. Regulators can ask our company to show how our drones have been looked after.

Interviewer: Who else at your company needs to know when a drone is out of service?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What tools or systems do you use when you do your work today?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When was the last time a regulator asked your company to show how drones had been looked after?

# Interview — a dispatcher

Interviewer: Could you walk me through your last working day as a dispatcher, starting from the moment you began until you finished?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: No problem, we can start smaller. What was the first thing you did when you started your last shift?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: That's fine. If you were explaining your job to a friend, what would you say you do?

Interviewee: As a dispatcher, I plan and run the flights for my company, and I am the licensed person responsible for each flight. I decide which drone flies and along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves. I can also call off a flight.

Interviewer: You mentioned you sign off each flight before it leaves. Can you tell me about the last flight you signed off, from when you first heard about it until it took off?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What do you look at when you decide which drone will fly a particular job?

Interviewee: I want help finding out which of my drones could get to where a job starts. A company may run a few hundred drones of several models from different manufacturers, and they differ in how much they can carry, how far they can fly on a full battery, which sensors they carry, and which charging connector they use. Choosing the drone and the way it flies is my legal responsibility, and our policy is that software never chooses a drone or a way for us.

Interviewer: How do you find out today which of your drones could get to where a job starts?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Is there anything you check yourself, by hand, because you don't fully trust the information you're given?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Who gives you the jobs that you plan and fly?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Can you think of a time when a flight you had signed off did not go as planned? What happened?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: You said you want help finding which of your drones could get to where a job starts. What makes that hard right now?

Interviewee: Several dispatchers plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and the same popular drones. Also, before and during a flight, things happen outside our control, like whether the load is ready, and a closure can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air.

Interviewer: What happens when two dispatchers want the same drone at the same time?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: You mentioned a closure can come into force while drones are already in the air. In that moment, what do you need to know?

Interviewee: I know that the authorities define zones where flying is prohibited and announce planned closures with a start and end time, as well as sudden ones that apply at once. These closures are often amended during the day, such as when an area is widened or an end time moves, and they can come into force while drones are already in the air.

Interviewer: When an amendment like that arrives during the day, what do you do first?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: You said your policy is that software never chooses a drone or a way for you. Why is that?

Interviewee: Choosing the drone and the way it flies is my legal responsibility as the dispatcher.

Interviewer: What would worry you if a new service got involved in that decision?

Interviewee: Choosing the drone and the way it flies is my legal responsibility as the dispatcher.

Interviewer: Who tells you when a drone is not fit to fly?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: You said things outside your control happen, like whether the load is ready. Can you give me an example of that?

Interviewee: Before and during a flight, things happen outside our control, such as whether the load is ready or not, whether the drone reaches the points of its job, and whether the drone arrives. Batteries also drain faster in cold and wind than planned, and radios can suffer from patchy coverage around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather.

Interviewer: If a drone does not arrive, what do you need to know right then?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: After you sign off a flight, who else needs to know about it?

Interviewee: Each company runs its own systems, such as billing and customer updates, that need to hear about what happens to its drones and jobs.

Interviewer: How do you feel about other companies knowing about your drones and jobs?

Interviewee: Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. We do accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

Interviewer: Can you give me an example of something about your company that you would never want another company to see?

Interviewee: Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business.

Interviewer: When did a closure last come into force while your drones were in the air?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: You mentioned batteries drain faster than planned in cold and wind. How do you deal with that today?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What goes wrong when several dispatchers plan for the same busy site?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What do you do when you lose radio contact with a drone?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Who do you contact first when something goes wrong with a flight in the air?

Interviewee: I don't know.

# Interview — a member of the platform's airspace desk

Interviewer: Could you walk me through an ordinary working day on the airspace desk, from the moment you start to the moment you finish?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: No problem. Think of your most recent shift instead. What was the first thing you did when you started?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: That's fine, we can start somewhere else. How would you describe what the airspace desk does to a friend who has never heard of it?

Interviewee: I keep the shared picture of the airspace for our shared service, which includes the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. My work is for all customer companies, and when a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.

Interviewer: Could you tell me about the last closure you entered, from the moment you heard about it?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Where does a closure announcement usually first reach you?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: That's okay. Let's try another angle: can you think of a day in the last few months when the work went badly?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Who do you talk to most often during your work?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: You mentioned wanting to know how much disruption a closure caused across customers. How do you find that out today?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Is there something about my questions that makes them hard to answer?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What worries you most about a new service replacing how you work now?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Is there anything in your work that you double-check yourself because you don't fully trust it?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: You said closures are announced by the authorities. What does one look like when you receive it?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Does anyone ask you for information or for changes to the airspace picture?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Imagine a closure caused trouble for a customer company. What is the first thing you would want to find out?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What did you work on yesterday?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What would you most like me to understand about your work?

Interviewee: I keep the shared picture of the airspace for our shared service, which consists of the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.

Interviewer: When you say "disruption", what does that look like for a customer company?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What is hardest about keeping the shared picture of the airspace up to date?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When you say "across customers", what would you need to see about each customer?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What happens when a closure is entered late?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What do you do right before you finish for the day?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: How do you learn that a closure has ended?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What do customer companies say to you about closures?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Is there anything you would like to tell me about your work that I haven't asked about?

Interviewee: I don't know.
=== END OF TRANSCRIPTS ===

Write the requirements for the service: what it must do, so that a team can build it and anyone can check whether it does. Rest every requirement on what the interviews say.

Write them as a list in YAML, in exactly this format, and nothing else:

```yaml
- id: DR-01
  requirement: >
    one thing the service must do, or must not do, and in which case
- id: DR-02
  requirement: >
    ...
```

Number the items DR-01, DR-02, and so on. Each item states one requirement in plain words.
